title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 48
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: A Room Anyone Could Enter
passages.text:
A. The coffee house mattered for what it was as a space rather than for what was drunk in it. For a small payment anyone respectably dressed could enter, sit among strangers, read what was on the tables and join a conversation already in progress — an arrangement with no real precedent in societies where sociable spaces were organised around rank, membership or invitation. The price of entry bought access to a room and to whoever happened to be in it.

B. Information was the actual commodity. Newspapers, price lists, shipping notices and pamphlets were provided and read aloud, and houses came to specialise: one frequented by merchants in a particular trade, another by writers, another by men interested in natural philosophy. Knowing where to go to hear a particular kind of news was a practical skill, and several institutions later formalised as exchanges, societies and insurance markets began as the regulars of a specific room.

C. The authorities distrusted them for reasons that were not unfounded. A place where strangers mixed, where news circulated faster than it could be checked, and where opinion formed collectively was genuinely difficult to supervise, and attempts to close or licence them were made repeatedly and largely failed. The objection was not to the beverage but to the conversation.

D. Their exclusions were as structural as their openness. Women were largely absent from these rooms in most cities while running many of the households whose commerce depended on them, and the price and the dress requirement kept out the poor. A space described at the time as open to all was open to a particular slice of the population, and the description has been repeated since with insufficient attention.

E. What replaced them is instructive about what they were for. As the specialised functions hardened into formal institutions — the exchange with members, the society with fellows, the newspaper with subscribers — the general room lost its purpose, because the information it circulated was now available elsewhere on more reliable terms. The institution died of its own success in generating successors.

F. The recurring interest in them is a search for a particular combination. A place that is cheap to enter, not organised around who you already know, where strangers can be encountered without arrangement and information moves informally, is a thing societies periodically notice they lack. The attempts to reconstruct it usually reproduce the sociability and not the function, which suggests the function depended on the scarcity of information rather than on the furniture.

passages.title: Animals That Chose Us
passages.text:
Domestication is usually described as something people did to animals, and the evidence for the earliest cases suggests a process much less deliberate than that. The animals that became domestic were disproportionately those that could tolerate proximity to humans, feed on what humans discarded, and breed in captivity, and the likeliest account of the first case is that wolves which scavenged around settlements were tolerated, that the least fearful bred most successfully near people, and that neither party planned anything.

The selection that follows is for temperament before anything else, and it drags a great deal with it. Experiments selecting wild animals for tameness alone, over many generations, have produced populations that also show changed coat colouring, shorter faces, smaller teeth, floppier ears, curled tails and altered breeding seasons — a suite of traits nobody selected for, appearing together. Something about the developmental system links them, which is why domestic animals of unrelated species resemble one another in ways their wild ancestors do not.

The proposed explanation is elegant and not fully established. Selecting for reduced fear may act on the cells that form part of the early embryo and later contribute to pigment, cartilage, jaw, ear and adrenal tissue, so a change affecting one produces changes across all of them. The idea accounts for the pattern better than any alternative and rests on evidence that is suggestive rather than conclusive, which is worth saying because the account is often repeated as settled.

Which species can be domesticated at all is more constrained than the number attempted suggests. An animal that will not breed under confinement, that panics catastrophically, that requires a diet nobody can supply in quantity, or whose social structure has no hierarchy a human can occupy is not a candidate however desirable it would be, and many large animals were tried and abandoned. The distribution of domesticable species across continents was uneven, and that unevenness had consequences.

The changes ran in both directions, which the usual framing obscures. Human genetics, settlement patterns, diet and disease exposure were all altered by living alongside animals — the ability to digest milk in adulthood spread in populations that kept dairy animals, and many of the infections that shaped human history crossed from domestic species. The relationship reorganised both parties.

Recent domestication looks quite different because the intention is now explicit. Selecting for milk yield, growth rate or docility with known tools and measured outcomes produces change far faster than any historical process, and it produces animals that would not survive without the system that maintains them. Whether that is a continuation of the same process or a different thing wearing its name is a question the word does not settle.

passages.title: Agreeing on the Shape of the Plug
passages.text:
A standard is an agreement to give up a choice, and almost every convenience of modern life rests on a large number of them. Screw threads, paper sizes, shipping container dimensions, character encodings, the voltage in a socket and the protocols moving this sentence are all decisions that could have been made differently and whose value comes entirely from being made the same way by everyone. The benefit is not in the specification but in the agreement.

Standards get established by three routes and the differences matter. Some are imposed by a government; some are negotiated in committees by the parties affected; and some are established by a product becoming so dominant that its way becomes the way. The third route is the fastest and the least accountable, since the resulting standard is controlled by whoever owns it and can be changed to suit them.

The economics are dominated by a property that ordinary goods do not have. A standard's value to each user rises with the number of other users, so adoption is self-reinforcing in both directions — a standard with a lead accelerates and one falling behind collapses, often regardless of technical merit. This is why the better specification frequently loses and why arguments about which is superior miss what actually decides the outcome.

The cost of the resulting lock-in is paid long after the choice. Once an industry has built equipment, trained people and written software around a standard, replacing it requires everyone to move at once, and no participant can move first without loss, so demonstrably poor standards persist for decades. Keyboard layouts, address formats, date conventions and units of measurement all include arrangements no one would choose now and no one can unilaterally leave.

Committees have a characteristic failure that is easy to recognise. A specification produced by parties with competing interests tends to include everyone's requirements, so it becomes large, contains optional features, and permits implementations that comply fully and do not work with one another. Optionality is the mechanism by which a standard fails while appearing to succeed, and the standards that work best are usually those that were small enough to leave little room for interpretation.

The open question is who should bear the cost of maintaining them. Standards bodies are funded by membership fees, by the companies that benefit most, or by governments, and each arrangement shapes what gets standardised and whose problems are addressed — small participants and users are systematically underrepresented in all three. The infrastructure everyone depends on is designed in rooms that most of the people affected have no way of entering.
